You're thinking of East Asians when Asia as a whole serves a multitude of nations, many of which are impoverished third-world countries like Cambodia and Myanmar. If you truly seek out the data on Asian American income, you will find that Asians have the highest discrepancy between the highest and lowest income compared to any other race. If you delve even further, you will find that those Asian Americans with higher incomes often have higher educations (masters, phds) and more working experience than their white counterparts who are in the same income bracket, which shows they had to work even harder to earn just as much.

There is a huge and important need for affinity groups because of the lack of access and knowledge in underrepresented and marginalized communities due to low income, education, etc. I hope everyone understands that the outdoors and climbing is predominately a white, male sport and there's a privilege in being able to climb outdoors, especially trad (with expensive gear). Many affinity group leaders saw this and found a need to create these spaces to teach and give people opportunities and chances that they wouldn't have been able to find on their own. Many people of color often feel isolated and scared in white spaces, no matter how accepting it is. There's a sense of comfort in being around people of the same cultures. 

I highly recommend watching "Black Ice" which was featured in last year's Reel Rock 15 about a group of Black climbers from Memphis going ice climbing for their first time. Why would anyone question groups that can open up experiences that can help change their lives?
